headline: South Carolina senator says health agency is breaking marijuana law
dek: Sen. Tom Davis told the Department of Public Health on 19 November to reschedule marijuana and start a 1980 patient programme; a reply is due by 19 December.
key_points: Republican Sen. Tom Davis wrote to acting health director Dr. Brannon Traxler on 19 November, saying the department is violating two state statutes.
One statute requires the department to match federal scheduling changes within 30 days of publication; Davis says that deadline passed on 28 May.
The other is a 1980 law that creates a marijuana programme for cancer and glaucoma patients and has never been fully put into effect.
Traxler acknowledged the letter and said the department will respond within 30 days; Davis also asked Attorney General Alan Wilson, the governor-elect, for a formal opinion.
body: South Carolina has no medical cannabis programme and its legislature has refused to pass one. A senior Republican senator now argues the state already has the law it needs, and that its health agency has been ignoring it since the spring.

In a two-page letter dated 19 November, Sen. Tom Davis of Beaufort told Dr. Brannon Traxler, acting director of the Department of Public Health, that the department is violating two state statutes. He asked for written answers to four questions within 30 days, which puts the deadline at 19 December, and asked Attorney General Alan Wilson for a formal opinion. The letter was reported by the Charleston City Paper, FITSNews and The Marijuana Herald.
## The 30-day rule

The first statute is Section 44-53-160(C) of the South Carolina Code. We read it. It says that when a substance is added, deleted or rescheduled under federal law, the director of the Department of Public Health "shall" make the same change within 30 days of the final order appearing in the Federal Register. The state change must be in substance identical to the federal order, and it has the force of law unless the General Assembly overturns it.

The federal order moving FDA-approved marijuana products and marijuana covered by qualifying state medical licences to Schedule III was signed on 23 April and published on 28 April. Davis counts 30 days from publication and says the department's deadline expired on 28 May. By our count, his letter was sent 175 days after that date.

Davis's argument is that the department has no choice in the matter. FITSNews, which obtained the letter, quotes him describing the agency's role as ministerial: whether South Carolina should depart from the federal decision is for the General Assembly alone.

He also points to what he sees as uneven practice. On 28 July, Traxler signed an order adopting the federal Schedule I classification of hexahydrocannabinol, or HHC, The Marijuana Herald reports. Davis's point is that the department used the statute when a federal decision tightened control over a cannabinoid and has not used it when a federal decision loosened control.
## The 1980 programme that never started

The second statute is the South Carolina Controlled Substances Therapeutic Research Act of 1980, which begins at Section 44-53-610. Section 44-53-630 establishes a therapeutic research programme inside the department, administered by the director, to distribute marijuana to certified cancer chemotherapy and radiology patients and to glaucoma patients.

The law tells the department to appoint a Patient Qualification Review Advisory Board, set up a way to certify patients and obtain marijuana through channels consistent with federal law, according to the three outlets' accounts of the letter. It has been on the books for 46 years and has never been fully carried out. Davis says the obstacle was marijuana's Schedule I status, and that the April order removed it.

He also tries to close off the most likely defence. Lack of funding does not excuse the department, he argues, citing a 2014 South Carolina Supreme Court ruling, Amisub of South Carolina v. South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control, The Marijuana Herald reports.
> Davis is not asking South Carolina to pass a medical cannabis law. He is saying it passed one in 1980.
## What Davis wants done

The demands are specific. Issue an order rescheduling marijuana in line with the federal order. Transmit and publish that order as the statute requires. Appoint the advisory board. Write the patient certification procedures. Take the steps needed to obtain marijuana lawfully.

The four questions ask why the department has not rescheduled marijuana, when it will issue the order, why the research programme has not been implemented, and when it will start appointing board members and obtaining marijuana. The letter was copied to Gov. Henry McMaster and to state health officials.
## The department's answer so far

It is short. Traxler replied by email that she had received the letter and that the department would respond within the 30 days requested, FITSNews reports. She did not say she accepts Davis's reading. The Charleston City Paper says the agency had not formally responded as of noon on 20 November, and recalls that when Davis first raised the point after the federal order, a spokesperson said the department was assessing the impact.
## Why the legal question is not simple

Davis has a plain-text argument on the first statute: the word is "shall" and the clock is 30 days. The harder question is what a conforming order would do. The federal order did not move marijuana as a whole to Schedule III. It moved FDA-approved products and marijuana handled under qualifying state medical licences. South Carolina has no such licences. An order "in substance identical" to the federal one would therefore create a Schedule III category that, today, nothing in the state falls into, apart from FDA-approved products.

That is our reading of the texts, not a finding by any court or by the attorney general. It is also why the second statute matters more to Davis's case. If the 1980 programme were stood up, it would be the state-authorised channel that the rescheduled category could attach to. Whether a research programme of that kind counts as a qualifying state medical licence under the federal order is a question none of the sources answers.

The 1980 law also limits itself to cancer and glaucoma patients and requires supply consistent with federal law. Even on Davis's reading it would be far narrower than the medical programmes in most states.
## The politics

Davis has sponsored medical cannabis bills for 11 years. Versions of his Compassionate Care Act passed the Republican-controlled Senate in 2022 and 2024 and died in the House. The Charleston City Paper notes that in May he said he would much prefer his own tightly drawn bill to the looser regime he believes existing law now requires, and blamed lawmakers' refusal to act for the result.

The request for an attorney general's opinion has an unusual feature. Wilson is also the governor-elect. The official asked to say what the health department must do will shortly be the governor it answers to.
## What to watch

The department's written response is due by 19 December. Watch for an opinion from the attorney general's office, which has no stated deadline in the reports we read. Watch whether Davis or a patient goes to court to compel action if the department declines. And watch the 2027 session, where Davis's letter gives House members a new choice: pass a programme they design, or risk having one read into a 46-year-old statute.
